clinicalPearls: A systemic bacterial (occasionally fungal or viral) infection in the first 28 days of life, conventionally split into early-onset (within roughly the first 72 hours, often maternally acquired) and late-onset (after 72 hours, frequently nosocomial or community-acquired).
Signs are notoriously nonspecific: temperature instability (fever or hypothermia), poor feeding, lethargy or irritability, respiratory distress, apnoea, tachycardia, and abdominal distension.

Group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli dominate early-onset disease; coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and Gram-negative organisms are common in late-onset disease, especially in preterm infants with indwelling lines.
Maternal risk factors include prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, maternal fever, and GBS colonisation without adequate intrapartum prophylaxis.
Blood culture is the diagnostic gold standard; a lumbar puncture should be considered because meningitis frequently coexists and may be missed.
Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics must be started promptly after cultures because deterioration can be rapid; the regimen is later narrowed to culture results.
Supportive care (thermoregulation, respiratory and haemodynamic support, glucose management) is as important as antimicrobials.
A low threshold for treatment is appropriate given nonspecific signs, but antibiotics are stopped early when cultures remain negative and the infant is well.
reference.pathophysiology: Neonates are relatively immunocompromised, with immature innate and adaptive defences, low immunoglobulin levels, and impaired neutrophil function. Organisms reach the infant by ascending or intrapartum transmission from the maternal genital tract in early-onset disease, or from the postnatal environment and invasive devices in late-onset disease. Once bloodstream invasion occurs, bacterial products trigger a systemic inflammatory response with cytokine release, endothelial injury, capillary leak, and impaired perfusion that can progress to septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and multi-organ dysfunction. The immature blood-brain barrier and limited containment of infection predispose to meningitis.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital heart disease with poor perfusion
Congenital viral infection (e.g. herpes simplex, cytomegalovirus)
additionalInvestigations: Complete blood count with differential and immature-to-total neutrophil ratio
C-reactive protein and/or procalcitonin, ideally serially
Lumbar puncture with CSF cell count, protein, glucose and culture
Urine culture (more relevant in late-onset disease)
Chest radiograph if respiratory signs are present
Blood glucose, electrolytes and blood gas to assess metabolic status
redFlags: Septic shock: poor perfusion, hypotension, prolonged capillary refill
Apnoea or worsening respiratory failure requiring support
Bulging fontanelle, seizures, or other signs suggesting meningitis
Petechiae, purpura, or bleeding suggesting disseminated intravascular coagulation
Persistent hypoglycaemia or profound metabolic acidosis
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on gestational age, organism, and speed of treatment; prompt therapy usually leads to recovery, but meningitis, shock, and prematurity carry higher mortality and risk of neurodevelopmental sequelae.
pitfalls: Attributing nonspecific signs to prematurity or feeding issues and delaying evaluation
Omitting a lumbar puncture and missing coexisting meningitis
Relying on a single normal inflammatory marker to exclude sepsis early in the illness
Failing to remove or consider infected central venous catheters in late-onset disease
management: Start prompt empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics after obtaining cultures, typically a penicillin (benzylpenicillin or ampicillin) plus an aminoglycoside for early-onset disease, because deterioration can be rapid
Tailor late-onset cover to likely nosocomial organisms and local patterns, adding anti-staphylococcal or glycopeptide cover, and broaden to a cephalosporin when meningitis is suspected
Narrow the regimen to culture and sensitivity results and add antifungal therapy if invasive fungal infection is identified
Provide supportive intensive care with fluid resuscitation, inotropes for septic shock, respiratory support and correction of disseminated intravascular coagulation
Perform lumbar puncture and treat coexisting meningitis with an appropriate agent and duration
Monitor blood cultures, inflammatory markers and clinical response to guide duration and de-escalation
Reinforce prevention through intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for maternal group B streptococcus colonisation
